t.5.40.1: Then, at the cries of the birds and the sound of trees being broken, all the inhabitants of Laṅkā became bewildered with fear.
t.5.40.3: Then, when their sleep had departed, the rākṣasīs with hideous faces saw that grove destroyed, and that heroic great monkey.
t.5.40.2: Terrified with fear, the beasts and birds fled and cried out loudly, and cruel portents appeared for the rākṣasas.
t.5.40.4: Seeing them, that mighty-armed one, great of spirit and great of strength, assumed an enormous form that struck fear into the rākṣasīs.
t.5.40.5: Then the rākṣasīs, seeing that monkey, huge of body, mighty in strength and resembling a mountain, questioned the daughter of Janaka.
t.5.40.6: Who is this, whose is he, and from where has he come? For what purpose has he come here, and how was a conversation held by you with him?
t.5.40.7: Tell us, O large-eyed one, and let there be no fear for you, O fortunate lady: what conversation did this one hold with you, O dark-eyed one?
t.5.40.8: Then the virtuous Sītā, lovely in every limb, said: "What means have I of recognizing rākṣasas, who can take on any form at will?"
t.5.40.9: You yourselves should know who he is and what he will do. Only a snake knows the feet of a snake; there is no doubt about this.
t.5.40.10: I too am afraid of him; I do not know who he is. I take him to be a rākṣasa who has come here, able to assume any form at will.
t.5.40.11: Hearing the words of Vaidehī, the rākṣasīs fled in haste; some stayed where they were, while others went to report it to Rāvaṇa.
t.5.40.12: Then, in the presence of Rāvaṇa, the rākṣasī women with their misshapen faces began to tell of the hideous and terrifying monkey.
t.5.40.13: O king, in the midst of the Aśoka grove stands a monkey of terrible form and boundless valor, who has held converse with Sītā.
t.5.40.14: And Sītā, daughter of Janaka, the doe-eyed one, though questioned by us in many ways, does not wish to reveal who that monkey is.
t.5.40.15: He may be a messenger of Vāsava, or a messenger of Vaiśravaṇa, or else one sent by Rāma out of a desire to search for Sītā.
t.5.40.16: But by that one of wondrous form, that charming pleasure grove of yours, crowded with herds of many kinds of animals, has been laid waste.
t.5.40.17: There is no spot there that he has not laid waste; only the place where Sītā, the Jānakī, stays has he not destroyed.
t.5.40.18: Is he not to be seen here because he is engaged in protecting Jānakī, or because of weariness? Yet what weariness could there be for him? It is she herself who has been protected by him.
t.5.40.19: But the tall śiṃśapā tree, rich in lovely shoots and leaves, beneath which Sītā herself had taken shelter, was carefully protected by him.
t.5.40.20: You should ordain a fierce punishment for that one of fierce form, by whom Sītā was spoken to and that grove was destroyed.
t.5.40.21: O lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas, who would dare to speak to Sītā, whom you have taken to your heart, unless he had already given up his life?
t.5.40.22: Hearing the words of the rākṣasīs, Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, blazed up like a fire fed with oblations, his eyes rolling with rage.
t.5.40.23: The greatly powerful one commanded heroic rākṣasas named Kiṃkaras, equal to himself, to seize Hanumān.
t.5.40.24: Of those swift and mighty Kiṃkaras, eighty thousand sallied forth from that mansion, bearing hammers and maces in their hands.
t.5.40.25: Big-bellied, huge-fanged, terrible in form and mighty in strength, all of them were bent on battle and eager to seize Hanūmān.
t.5.40.26: Approaching that monkey who stood stationed upon the gateway, they, with great speed, rushed upon him like moths upon a fire.
t.5.40.27: They struck the best of monkeys with variegated maces, with iron bars bound with golden bands, and with arrows resembling the sun.
t.5.40.28: Hanumān too, radiant and glorious, resembling a mountain, lashed his tail upon the ground and roared with a mighty sound.
t.5.40.29: At the sound of his roaring they became stricken with fear, and they saw Hanūmān towering high like a cloud at twilight.
t.5.40.30: Then those rākṣasas, made fearless by their master's command, rushed upon the monkey from all sides with varied and terrible weapons.
t.5.40.31: Surrounded on all sides by those heroes, he, the mighty one, laid hold of a fearsome iron bar that rested on the gateway.
t.5.40.33: Like the son of Vinatā seizing a writhing serpent, the heroic Māruti grasped him firmly and roamed through the sky.
t.5.40.32: Taking up that iron club, he struck down the night-roaming demons.
t.5.40.34: Having slain the Kiṃkara rākṣasas, that hero, the son of Māruta, eager for battle, again took his stand at the archway.
t.5.40.35: Then some rākṣasas there, freed from that terror, reported to Rāvaṇa that all the Kiṃkaras had been slain.
t.5.40.36: Hearing that the mighty host of rākṣasas had been slain, the king, his eyes rolling, gave orders to the son of Prahasta, who was unequalled in valour and very hard to conquer in battle.
